tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

## 14. Direct exports versus the jobs/storage platform

[39 — Implement CSV and BibTeX Reporting Exports](39-csv-bibtex-exports.md) requires immediate streaming without persistence, jobs, retry, expiry, or artifact revocation. [40 — Implement Python and R Statistical Analysis Exports](40-python-r-exports.md) also streams ZIPs without retention and does not execute Python/R on the server.

Generic jobs/storage tasks mention persisted exports. The plan keeps the specific contracts visible; record the integration decision without forcing jobs/storage into these endpoints.

CSV/BibTeX permissions say every application user, but the API requires project/export authorization. Define whether this covers members, Guests, or an authorized public audience.

## 15. Imports: intake, parsing, duplicates, and rollback

[27 — Implement Secure Import Storage and Project Job Progress](27-import-intake.md) excludes parsing/mapping/metadata/deduplication/commit/rollback and limits states, but its acceptance criteria mention complete results/duplicates. The guide preserves the intake boundary.

[29 — Implement BibTeX and EndNote Import Parsers](29-bibler-import.md) excludes deduplication/rollback implementation, but acceptance criteria require sharing those workflows with CSV. [28 — Provide one CSV Import page organised into progressive sections.](28-csv-import.md) also mentions rollback in permissions without defining execution. No complete standalone tickets for these features exist in the consulted inventory.

Temporary files start with a 24-hour storage TTL; define behavior for active batches that exceed it. Safety cleanup is storage-level, with no dedicated application job in this task.

## 16. Statistics and legacy parity

[32 — Implement Screening Progress Dashboard and Agreement Statistics](32-screening-metrics.md) does not specify the Kappa variant, missing-data handling, or criteria denominators. Define formulas and edge cases before treating statistics as validated.

[40 — Implement Python and R Statistical Analysis Exports](40-python-r-exports.md) requires legacy analysis families but provides no templates. [29 — Implement BibTeX and EndNote Import Parsers](29-bibler-import.md) requires approved fixtures and the private BiBler contract. Locate those materials; do not invent parity from the description.

## 17. Dependencies without complete tickets

[24 — Implement Project Paper List](24-paper-list.md) shows Edit/Delete but specifies only reads. Authorship/order editing belongs to Paper editing and is referenced elsewhere, without its own record among the 42 tasks.

Shared email, anti-abuse protection, frontend scaffolding, deduplication, and rollback also require an existing implementation or defined additional scope. A missing ticket does not authorize ignoring a dependency or marking features complete.

## 18. Empty fields and proposed checks

The source lacks Acceptance criteria for runtime config, Docker Compose, Control Prisma, Project Prisma, API shell, project resolver, profile, Authors/Affiliations, and Paper List. Each guide flags this absence and offers proposed checks.

Empty Jobs behavior/Audit fields do not remove job/audit requirements stated elsewhere. Each page's status is only a snapshot from the consultation, not a verification of the code.

## 19. Unit-test placement

The supplied mandatory tree explicitly includes tests/e2e, tests/integration, tests/migration, tests/fixtures, and packages/test-utils, but no unit-test location. No existing unit files were found in this submodule on 2026-09-27. Preserve the specified categories; request a placement decision when introducing the first unit suite. Do not silently add tests/unit or relocate integration tests beside application source. See [testing-policy.md](../testing-policy.md).

1	# Local Docker Compose stack for ReLiS — ONE documented startup command
2	# for the seven service responsibilities required by this sub-issue (see
3	# docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md for prerequisites, endpoints,
4	# shutdown, and honest limitations; docs/architecture/local-stack-inventory.md
5	# for the application startup contracts this stack reuses unchanged):
6	#
7	#   1. apps/web   (Next.js, existing `dev` command)
8	#   2. apps/api   (Hono, existing `dev` command)
9	#   3. apps/worker (existing `dev` command — tsx watch; logs and stays
10	#      alive, does NOT process jobs — see worker/worker-related comments
11	#      below and the inventory doc §3.3/§7)
12	#   4. postgres   (one server, two disposable databases: Control DB +
13	#      project-test target — provisioned via migrate-control/migrate-project)
14	#   5. nginx      (the only published entry point for web + API)
15	#   6. storage    (SeaweedFS, S3-compatible endpoint — no application
16	#      adapter exists yet; this provisions the infrastructure only)
17	#   7. mailhog    (local mail capture — prescribed by
18	#      context/project-structure.md's docker/mailhog/ entry; no
19	#      application mail adapter exists yet either)
20	#
21	# This stack is local-development only: no production target, no TLS, no
22	# CI wiring, no business schema, no queue consumer, no storage/mail
23	# adapter. The background-job backend (pg-boss vs. BullMQ) remains
24	# undecided — apps/worker's dev command here is the same idle process
25	# described in the inventory doc; running it in Compose is not evidence
26	# of job processing, and no Redis (or any BullMQ-only dependency) is
27	# added.
28	#
29	# Startup:  docker compose up --build
30	# Shutdown: docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --remove-orphans
31	#             -> removes containers/network, KEEPS both named volumes and
32	#                all local data; `up -d` afterward recreates with data
33	#                intact.
34	# Reset:    docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --volumes --remove-orphans
35	#             -> ALSO deletes this project's postgres-data and
36	#                storage-data volumes. Irreversible: both logical
37	#                databases and every stored object at once. No backup
38	#                exists. Never part of ordinary startup, and never a
39	#                broad `docker ... prune` (that reaches other projects).
40	# Full lifecycle table, persistence inventory, and clean-recreation
41	# steps: docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md
42	#        ("Persistence, lifecycle, and reset").
43	
44	networks:
45	  relis:
46	    name: ${COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME:-relis}-net
47	
48	# Persistent local data — both DISPOSABLE. Compose prefixes each with the
49	# project name (`relis_postgres-data` for a default startup from this
50	# directory), which is what keeps two Compose projects from ever sharing
51	# one. Deliberately neither `external:` nor explicitly `name:`d: an
52	# external volume would be a pre-existing resource outside this stack's
53	# lifecycle, and a fixed name would make every project collide on the
54	# same data. No host path and no production endpoint is involved.
55	# See docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md "Persistence, lifecycle,
56	# and reset" for what each holds and what a reset destroys.
57	volumes:
58	  # The whole PostgreSQL cluster: BOTH logical databases (the Control DB
59	  # and the project-test target) plus server-wide state. One server, one
60	  # volume, two databases — a volume per database is deliberately NOT a
61	  # requirement here.
62	  postgres-data:
63	  # SeaweedFS's entire single-node state in one directory (master
64	  # metadata, object/volume files, filer metadata) — i.e. every
65	  # non-production bucket and object.
66	  storage-data:
67	
68	services:
69	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
70	  # PostgreSQL: one server, two disposable local databases (Control DB +
71	  # project-test target). Not published to the host — see
72	  # docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md for how to reach it when a
73	  # documented development endpoint is genuinely needed (docker compose
74	  # exec).
75	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
76	  postgres:
77	    image: postgres:17-alpine
78	    environment:
79	      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-relis}
80	      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-changeme}
81	      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-relis_control}
82	      PROJECT_TEST_DB_NAME: ${PROJECT_TEST_DB_NAME:-relis_project_example}
83	    volumes:
84	      # Named volume, never a host bind mount: database data must never
85	      # land at a path inside this repository (see the `volumes:` block
86	      # above). ./docker/postgres/init is read-only committed SQL, and
87	      # the official image runs it ONLY on a genuinely first init (empty
88	      # data directory) — so changing POSTGRES_DB/PROJECT_TEST_DB_NAME
89	      # against an existing volume does not create the new database.
90	      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
91	      - ./docker/postgres/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro
92	    healthcheck:
93	      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U \"$$POSTGRES_USER\" -d \"$$POSTGRES_DB\""]
94	      interval: 5s
95	      timeout: 5s
96	      retries: 10
97	    networks: [relis]
98	
99	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
100	  # One-shot provisioning: runs the EXISTING migration entry point
101	  # (packages/database/src/migrate.ts) against each disposable database
102	  # target in turn. Both Prisma schemas define zero models today — this
103	  # proves the CONTROL_DATABASE_URL / PROJECT_DATABASE_URL contract and
104	  # the two distinct database targets wire up correctly; it does not add
105	  # any business schema. Reuses docker/worker/Dockerfile's image (see that
106	  # file's header comment for why).
107	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
108	  migrate-control:
109	    build:
110	      context: .
111	      dockerfile: docker/worker/Dockerfile
112	    command: ["sh", "-c", "pnpm --filter @relis/config build && pnpm --filter @relis/database run migrate control"]
113	    environment:
114	      NODE_ENV: development
115	      CONTROL_DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:-relis}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-changeme}@postgres:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:-relis_control}
116	    depends_on:
117	      postgres:
118	        condition: service_healthy
119	    networks: [relis]
120	    restart: "no"
121	
122	  migrate-project:
123	    build:
124	      context: .
125	      dockerfile: docker/worker/Dockerfile
126	    command: ["sh", "-c", "pnpm --filter @relis/config build && pnpm --filter @relis/database run migrate project"]
127	    environment:
128	      NODE_ENV: development
129	      PROJECT_DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:-relis}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-changeme}@postgres:5432/${PROJECT_TEST_DB_NAME:-relis_project_example}
130	    depends_on:
131	      postgres:
132	        condition: service_healthy
133	    networks: [relis]
134	    restart: "no"
135	
136	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
137	  # apps/api (Hono). Binds API_HOST=0.0.0.0 by default (already
138	  # container-to-container compatible — inventory doc §3.1). Its port is
139	  # never published to the host: reachable only via nginx's /api/ prefix.
140	  # No depends_on a database: apps/api does not connect to one today
141	  # (inventory doc §3.1/§7) — not invented here.
142	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
143	  api:
144	    build:
145	      context: .
146	      dockerfile: docker/api/Dockerfile
147	    environment:
148	      NODE_ENV: development
149	      API_PORT: 3001
150	      API_HOST: 0.0.0.0
151	      # Same-origin via nginx in normal use (see nginx.conf's header
152	      # comment); set defensively in case anything calls apps/api
153	      # directly during development.
154	      API_CORS_ORIGIN: http://localhost:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT:-8080}
155	    volumes:
156	      - ./apps/api/src:/app/apps/api/src
157	      - ./packages/config/src:/app/packages/config/src
158	    healthcheck:
159	      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:3001/health"]
160	      interval: 5s
161	      timeout: 5s
162	      retries: 10
163	      start_period: 15s
164	    networks: [relis]
165	
166	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
167	  # apps/web (Next.js dev). NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL points at nginx's own
168	  # published port with an /api prefix — a browser-reachable address, NOT
169	  # the internal "api" Compose hostname (see docs/architecture/
170	  # docker-compose-stack.md "Internal vs. browser-public addresses").
171	  # Never published directly: reachable only through nginx.
172	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
173	  web:
174	    build:
175	      context: .
176	      dockerfile: docker/web/Dockerfile
177	    environment:
178	      NODE_ENV: development
179	      WEB_PORT: 3000
180	      NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: http://localhost:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT:-8080}/api
181	    volumes:
182	      - ./apps/web/src:/app/apps/web/src
183	      - ./apps/web/public:/app/apps/web/public
184	      - ./packages/config/src:/app/packages/config/src
185	    healthcheck:
186	      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:3000/"]
187	      interval: 10s
188	      timeout: 5s
189	      retries: 10
190	      start_period: 20s
191	    networks: [relis]
192	
193	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
194	  # apps/worker (existing DEV command — tsx watch). start logs and exits;
195	  # dev's tsx watch supervisor stays alive after the same log-and-return.
196	  # NEITHER mode processes jobs (no queue consumer exists — inventory doc
197	  # §3.3/§7). No healthcheck: there is no real readiness signal to check,
198	  # and fabricating one (e.g. "process is running") would not be evidence
199	  # of job processing — see this task's explicit boundary on that point.
200	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
201	  worker:
202	    build:
203	      context: .
204	      dockerfile: docker/worker/Dockerfile
205	    environment:
206	      NODE_ENV: development
207	    volumes:
208	      - ./apps/worker/src:/app/apps/worker/src
209	      - ./packages/config/src:/app/packages/config/src
210	    networks: [relis]
211	
212	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
213	  # Reverse proxy — the ONLY published entry point for web + API. Bound
214	  # to loopback. See docker/nginx/nginx.conf for routing.
215	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
216	  nginx:
217	    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
218	    volumes:
219	      - ./docker/nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
220	    ports:
221	      - "127.0.0.1:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT:-8080}:80"
222	    depends_on:
223	      - web
224	      - api
225	    healthcheck:
226	      # 127.0.0.1, not "localhost": nginx:alpine's musl resolver returns
227	      # ::1 before 127.0.0.1 for "localhost" inside this container (real,
228	      # reproducible — found via actual verification, not theoretical),
229	      # and this nginx.conf's `listen 80;` only binds IPv4, so a
230	      # "localhost" request here gets connection-refused even though
231	      # nginx is serving correctly. Does not affect host access (Docker
232	      # Desktop's own port-forwarding resolves "localhost" to the
233	      # published 127.0.0.1 mapping correctly on this host) or any
234	      # container-to-container traffic (which always addresses this
235	      # service by its Compose name "nginx", never "localhost").
236	      test: ["CMD", "wget", "--spider", "-q", "http://127.0.0.1/nginx-health"]
237	      interval: 5s
238	      timeout: 5s
239	      retries: 5
240	    networks: [relis]
241	
242	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
243	  # Local mail capture. MailHog is prescribed by
244	  # context/project-structure.md's docker/mailhog/ entry (not an open
245	  # choice — see docs/architecture/local-stack-inventory.md §8). Only its
246	  # web UI is published, as a documented development-only endpoint for
247	  # inspecting captured mail; SMTP submission (1025) stays internal since
248	  # no application mail adapter exists yet to submit through it.
249	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
250	  mailhog:
251	    image: mailhog/mailhog:v1.0.1
252	    ports:
253	      - "127.0.0.1:${MAILHOG_UI_PORT:-8025}:8025"
254	    # No healthcheck: MailHog's official image is commonly built as a
255	    # minimal/near-scratch Go binary with no shell or wget bundled, and
256	    # that could not be confirmed without a registry pull in this
257	    # environment (see docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md's "Known
258	    # limitations"). Fabricating a healthcheck command that might simply
259	    # fail with "not found" — and so be misread as "unhealthy" — would be
260	    # worse than having none; readiness is instead polled from the test
261	    # client's own side (see stack-smoke.test.ts).
262	    networks: [relis]
263	
264	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
265	  # Local object storage. SeaweedFS in single-node "weed server" mode
266	  # (master + volume + filer + its S3 gateway, all in one process) — an
267	  # explicit infrastructure choice approved for this task (not MinIO/
268	  # LocalStack/Azurite, and not a production provider decision). The S3
269	  # gateway requires the development-only identity in
270	  # docker/storage/s3-identities.json (mounted read-only) for every
271	  # request — no anonymous access. No application storage adapter exists
272	  # yet (inventory doc §6.3); this provisions the service only, per this
273	  # task's explicit "service availability is separate from application
274	  # integration" boundary.
275	  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
276	  storage:
277	    image: chrislusf/seaweedfs:3.71
278	    command:
279	      - server
280	      - -dir=/data
281	      - -ip=storage
282	      - -master.port=9333
283	      - -volume.port=8080
284	      - -filer.port=8888
285	      - -s3
286	      - -s3.port=8333
287	      - -s3.config=/etc/seaweedfs/s3-identities.json
288	    volumes:
289	      # Named volume, never a host bind mount — same reason as postgres
290	      # above. The identities file is read-only committed development
291	      # configuration, not data.
292	      - storage-data:/data
293	      - ./docker/storage/s3-identities.json:/etc/seaweedfs/s3-identities.json:ro
294	    ports:
295	      - "127.0.0.1:${SEAWEEDFS_S3_PORT:-8333}:8333"
296	    healthcheck:
297	      # A plain TCP check on 8333 (the S3 gateway port, via BusyBox nc -z
298	      # — curl is not present in this image, and BusyBox wget's exit code
299	      # cannot distinguish "got a 403" from "connection refused", both
300	      # confirmed by direct inspection), not an HTTP check against the
301	      # master's /cluster/status on 9333. This matters because this
302	      # service's own startup logs show the S3 API only starts LISTENING
303	      # on 8333 after its internal filer connection succeeds (there is a
304	      # brief window after the master itself is ready where the S3 side
305	      # is not yet listening) — checking the master alone let Docker
306	      # report "healthy" before a real S3 request could reliably
307	      # succeed, reproducibly causing "socket closed" on an authenticated
308	      # PUT issued right after. 127.0.0.1, not "localhost": this
309	      # Alpine-based image's /etc/hosts maps "localhost" to ::1 only.
310	      # Does not affect container-to-container traffic, which always
311	      # addresses this service by its Compose name "storage".
312	      test: ["CMD", "nc", "-z", "127.0.0.1", "8333"]
313	      interval: 5s
314	      timeout: 5s
315	      retries: 10
316	      start_period: 10s
317	    networks: [relis]

# Local Docker Compose stack for ReLiS — ONE documented startup command
# for the seven service responsibilities required by this sub-issue (see
# docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md for prerequisites, endpoints,
# shutdown, and honest limitations; docs/architecture/local-stack-inventory.md
# for the application startup contracts this stack reuses unchanged):
#
#   1. apps/web   (Next.js, existing `dev` command)
#   2. apps/api   (Hono, existing `dev` command)
#   3. apps/worker (existing `dev` command — tsx watch; logs and stays
#      alive, does NOT process jobs — see worker/worker-related comments
#      below and the inventory doc §3.3/§7)
#   4. postgres   (one server, two disposable databases: Control DB +
#      project-test target — provisioned via migrate-control/migrate-project)
#   5. nginx      (the only published entry point for web + API)
#   6. storage    (SeaweedFS, S3-compatible endpoint — no application
#      adapter exists yet; this provisions the infrastructure only)
#   7. mailhog    (local mail capture — prescribed by
#      context/project-structure.md's docker/mailhog/ entry; no
#      application mail adapter exists yet either)
#
# This stack is local-development only: no production target, no TLS, no
# CI wiring, no business schema, no queue consumer, no storage/mail
# adapter. The background-job backend (pg-boss vs. BullMQ) remains
# undecided — apps/worker's dev command here is the same idle process
# described in the inventory doc; running it in Compose is not evidence
# of job processing, and no Redis (or any BullMQ-only dependency) is
# added.
#
# Startup:  docker compose up --build
# Shutdown: docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --remove-orphans
#             -> removes containers/network, KEEPS both named volumes and
#                all local data; `up -d` afterward recreates with data
#                intact.
# Reset:    docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --volumes --remove-orphans
#             -> ALSO deletes this project's postgres-data and
#                storage-data volumes. Irreversible: both logical
#                databases and every stored object at once. No backup
#                exists. Never part of ordinary startup, and never a
#                broad `docker ... prune` (that reaches other projects).
# Full lifecycle table, persistence inventory, and clean-recreation
# steps: docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md
#        ("Persistence, lifecycle, and reset").

networks:
  relis:
    name: ${COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME:-relis}-net

# Persistent local data — both DISPOSABLE. Compose prefixes each with the
# project name (`relis_postgres-data` for a default startup from this
# directory), which is what keeps two Compose projects from ever sharing
# one. Deliberately neither `external:` nor explicitly `name:`d: an
# external volume would be a pre-existing resource outside this stack's
# lifecycle, and a fixed name would make every project collide on the
# same data. No host path and no production endpoint is involved.
# See docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md "Persistence, lifecycle,
# and reset" for what each holds and what a reset destroys.
volumes:
  # The whole PostgreSQL cluster: BOTH logical databases (the Control DB
  # and the project-test target) plus server-wide state. One server, one
  # volume, two databases — a volume per database is deliberately NOT a
  # requirement here.
  postgres-data:
  # SeaweedFS's entire single-node state in one directory (master
  # metadata, object/volume files, filer metadata) — i.e. every
  # non-production bucket and object.
  storage-data:

services:
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  # PostgreSQL: one server, two disposable local databases (Control DB +
  # project-test target). Not published to the host — see
  # docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md for how to reach it when a
  # documented development endpoint is genuinely needed (docker compose
  # exec).
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  postgres:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-relis}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-changeme}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-relis_control}
      PROJECT_TEST_DB_NAME: ${PROJECT_TEST_DB_NAME:-relis_project_example}
    volumes:
      # Named volume, never a host bind mount: database data must never
      # land at a path inside this repository (see the `volumes:` block
      # above). ./docker/postgres/init is read-only committed SQL, and
      # the official image runs it ONLY on a genuinely first init (empty
      # data directory) — so changing POSTGRES_DB/PROJECT_TEST_DB_NAME
      # against an existing volume does not create the new database.
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./docker/postgres/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U \"$$POSTGRES_USER\" -d \"$$POSTGRES_DB\""]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
    networks: [relis]

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  # One-shot provisioning: runs the EXISTING migration entry point
  # (packages/database/src/migrate.ts) against each disposable database
  # target in turn. Both Prisma schemas define zero models today — this
  # proves the CONTROL_DATABASE_URL / PROJECT_DATABASE_URL contract and
  # the two distinct database targets wire up correctly; it does not add
  # any business schema. Reuses docker/worker/Dockerfile's image (see that
  # file's header comment for why).
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  migrate-control:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: docker/worker/Dockerfile
    command: ["sh", "-c", "pnpm --filter @relis/config build && pnpm --filter @relis/database run migrate control"]
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: development
      CONTROL_DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:-relis}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-changeme}@postgres:5432/${POSTGRES_DB:-relis_control}
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks: [relis]
    restart: "no"

  migrate-project:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: docker/worker/Dockerfile
    command: ["sh", "-c", "pnpm --filter @relis/config build && pnpm --filter @relis/database run migrate project"]
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: development
      PROJECT_DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER:-relis}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-changeme}@postgres:5432/${PROJECT_TEST_DB_NAME:-relis_project_example}
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks: [relis]
    restart: "no"

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  # apps/api (Hono). Binds API_HOST=0.0.0.0 by default (already
  # container-to-container compatible — inventory doc §3.1). Its port is
  # never published to the host: reachable only via nginx's /api/ prefix.
  # No depends_on a database: apps/api does not connect to one today
  # (inventory doc §3.1/§7) — not invented here.
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: docker/api/Dockerfile
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: development
      API_PORT: 3001
      API_HOST: 0.0.0.0
      # Same-origin via nginx in normal use (see nginx.conf's header
      # comment); set defensively in case anything calls apps/api
      # directly during development.
      API_CORS_ORIGIN: http://localhost:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT:-8080}
    volumes:
      - ./apps/api/src:/app/apps/api/src
      - ./packages/config/src:/app/packages/config/src
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:3001/health"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 15s
    networks: [relis]

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  # apps/web (Next.js dev). NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL points at nginx's own
  # published port with an /api prefix — a browser-reachable address, NOT
  # the internal "api" Compose hostname (see docs/architecture/
  # docker-compose-stack.md "Internal vs. browser-public addresses").
  # Never published directly: reachable only through nginx.
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  web:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: docker/web/Dockerfile
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: development
      WEB_PORT: 3000
      NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: http://localhost:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT:-8080}/api
    volumes:
      - ./apps/web/src:/app/apps/web/src
      - ./apps/web/public:/app/apps/web/public
      - ./packages/config/src:/app/packages/config/src
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:3000/"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 20s
    networks: [relis]

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  # apps/worker (existing DEV command — tsx watch). start logs and exits;
  # dev's tsx watch supervisor stays alive after the same log-and-return.
  # NEITHER mode processes jobs (no queue consumer exists — inventory doc
  # §3.3/§7). No healthcheck: there is no real readiness signal to check,
  # and fabricating one (e.g. "process is running") would not be evidence
  # of job processing — see this task's explicit boundary on that point.
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  worker:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: docker/worker/Dockerfile
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: development
    volumes:
      - ./apps/worker/src:/app/apps/worker/src
      - ./packages/config/src:/app/packages/config/src
    networks: [relis]

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Reverse proxy — the ONLY published entry point for web + API. Bound
  # to loopback. See docker/nginx/nginx.conf for routing.
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    volumes:
      - ./docker/nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT:-8080}:80"
    depends_on:
      - web
      - api
    healthcheck:
      # 127.0.0.1, not "localhost": nginx:alpine's musl resolver returns
      # ::1 before 127.0.0.1 for "localhost" inside this container (real,
      # reproducible — found via actual verification, not theoretical),
      # and this nginx.conf's `listen 80;` only binds IPv4, so a
      # "localhost" request here gets connection-refused even though
      # nginx is serving correctly. Does not affect host access (Docker
      # Desktop's own port-forwarding resolves "localhost" to the
      # published 127.0.0.1 mapping correctly on this host) or any
      # container-to-container traffic (which always addresses this
      # service by its Compose name "nginx", never "localhost").
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "--spider", "-q", "http://127.0.0.1/nginx-health"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
    networks: [relis]

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Local mail capture. MailHog is prescribed by
  # context/project-structure.md's docker/mailhog/ entry (not an open
  # choice — see docs/architecture/local-stack-inventory.md §8). Only its
  # web UI is published, as a documented development-only endpoint for
  # inspecting captured mail; SMTP submission (1025) stays internal since
  # no application mail adapter exists yet to submit through it.
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  mailhog:
    image: mailhog/mailhog:v1.0.1
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${MAILHOG_UI_PORT:-8025}:8025"
    # No healthcheck: MailHog's official image is commonly built as a
    # minimal/near-scratch Go binary with no shell or wget bundled, and
    # that could not be confirmed without a registry pull in this
    # environment (see docs/architecture/docker-compose-stack.md's "Known
    # limitations"). Fabricating a healthcheck command that might simply
    # fail with "not found" — and so be misread as "unhealthy" — would be
    # worse than having none; readiness is instead polled from the test
    # client's own side (see stack-smoke.test.ts).
    networks: [relis]

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Local object storage. SeaweedFS in single-node "weed server" mode
  # (master + volume + filer + its S3 gateway, all in one process) — an
  # explicit infrastructure choice approved for this task (not MinIO/
  # LocalStack/Azurite, and not a production provider decision). The S3
  # gateway requires the development-only identity in
  # docker/storage/s3-identities.json (mounted read-only) for every
  # request — no anonymous access. No application storage adapter exists
  # yet (inventory doc §6.3); this provisions the service only, per this
  # task's explicit "service availability is separate from application
  # integration" boundary.
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
  storage:
    image: chrislusf/seaweedfs:3.71
    command:
      - server
      - -dir=/data
      - -ip=storage
      - -master.port=9333
      - -volume.port=8080
      - -filer.port=8888
      - -s3
      - -s3.port=8333
      - -s3.config=/etc/seaweedfs/s3-identities.json
    volumes:
      # Named volume, never a host bind mount — same reason as postgres
      # above. The identities file is read-only committed development
      # configuration, not data.
      - storage-data:/data
      - ./docker/storage/s3-identities.json:/etc/seaweedfs/s3-identities.json:ro
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${SEAWEEDFS_S3_PORT:-8333}:8333"
    healthcheck:
      # A plain TCP check on 8333 (the S3 gateway port, via BusyBox nc -z
      # — curl is not present in this image, and BusyBox wget's exit code
      # cannot distinguish "got a 403" from "connection refused", both
      # confirmed by direct inspection), not an HTTP check against the
      # master's /cluster/status on 9333. This matters because this
      # service's own startup logs show the S3 API only starts LISTENING
      # on 8333 after its internal filer connection succeeds (there is a
      # brief window after the master itself is ready where the S3 side
      # is not yet listening) — checking the master alone let Docker
      # report "healthy" before a real S3 request could reliably
      # succeed, reproducibly causing "socket closed" on an authenticated
      # PUT issued right after. 127.0.0.1, not "localhost": this
      # Alpine-based image's /etc/hosts maps "localhost" to ::1 only.
      # Does not affect container-to-container traffic, which always
      # addresses this service by its Compose name "storage".
      test: ["CMD", "nc", "-z", "127.0.0.1", "8333"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 10s
    networks: [relis]

content.content:
1	# Local Docker Compose stack
2	
3	Implements local sub-issues [02.02 — Define services and shared
4	configuration, including the Control DB and per-project test
5	databases](../../../context/notion-tasks/sub-issues/02-02.md) and
6	[02.03 — Configure local persistent volumes and exclude them from version
7	control](../../../context/notion-tasks/sub-issues/02-03.md) (parent: [02
8	— Add Docker Compose local stack](../../../context/notion-tasks/02-docker-compose.md)).
9	Builds directly on [the local-stack inventory](local-stack-inventory.md)
10	from the preceding sub-issue — read that document first for the
11	application startup contracts this stack reuses unchanged (it does not
12	re-derive them here). Data persistence, the stop/start/recreate/reset
13	lifecycle, and what a reset destroys are in
14	["Persistence, lifecycle, and reset"](#persistence-lifecycle-and-reset).
15	
16	## Scope
17	
18	One Compose file (`docker-compose.yml`, repository root) defines all seven
19	required service responsibilities as real processes/containers:
20	
21	1. `web` — the existing Next.js app, `dev` command.
22	2. `api` — the existing Hono API, `dev` command.
23	3. `worker` — the existing worker **development** process (`tsx watch`) —
24	   not `start`, and not a job processor either way (see "Known
25	   limitations" below).
26	4. `postgres` — one PostgreSQL server, two disposable databases: the
27	   Control DB and a project-test target.
28	5. `nginx` — the reverse proxy; the only published entry point for the
29	   browser.
30	6. `storage` — SeaweedFS, S3-compatible endpoint, single-node mode.
31	7. `mailhog` — local mail capture.
32	
33	Everything here is local-development only. No production target, no TLS,
34	no CI wiring, no business schema, no queue consumer, no storage/mail
35	*application* adapter. `docker-compose.dev.yml` / `docker-compose.test.yml`
36	were not created: `docker-compose.yml` already runs dev-mode processes
37	with live-reload mounts (see "Development mounts" below), so a separate
38	dev overlay was not needed for this sub-issue's scope, and the test
39	harness (`tests/integration/docker-compose/`) achieves isolation via a
40	unique `-p` project name and either a pre-picked free host port
41	(`NGINX_HTTP_PORT` — required because that value is baked into
42	`NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` at container start) or an ephemeral host port
43	discovered after startup (`MAILHOG_UI_PORT`/`SEAWEEDFS_S3_PORT`, neither
44	read by any application code) instead of a dedicated compose file — see
45	"Tests" below.
46	
47	## Prerequisites
48	
49	- Docker Engine with the Compose V2 CLI plugin (the `docker compose`
50	  subcommand, not the legacy standalone `docker-compose` V1 binary), with
51	  a Linux-container backend. **Verified by real execution** (Docker
52	  Desktop 29.8.2 / `docker compose` plugin v5.5.1, Windows host,
53	  WSL2/Linux-container engine) — see the final report for sub-issue #47
54	  for the exact commands and results. Earlier drafts of this document
55	  were written before Docker was available and said so explicitly; that
56	  caveat no longer applies.
57	- No `pnpm`/Node install needed on the host — every app container installs
58	  its own dependencies at image-build time (`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`
59	  against the committed `pnpm-lock.yaml`).
60	- Copy `.env.example` to `.env` at the repository root (same convention as
61	  the existing runtime-config setup — see `README.md` "Runtime
62	  configuration"). Every value in it is a development-only placeholder.
63	- Only for the real-browser check (`tests/e2e/docker-compose/`):
64	  Playwright's Chromium browser binary must be installed
65	  (`pnpm exec playwright install chromium`). **Now installed and
66	  verified** in the environment that ran the sub-issue #47 real
67	  verification (`pnpm run test:e2e` passed with a real Chromium
68	  instance). Installing it remains a deliberate, separately-authorized
69	  step in a fresh checkout — this repository's tooling does not do it on
70	  your own behalf automatically.
71	
72	## Startup
73	
74	```bash
75	docker compose up --build
76	```
77	
78	First run builds `web`, `api`, and `worker`'s images (each installs the
79	full pnpm workspace and bakes an initial `@relis/config` build — see
80	"Clean-checkout startup" below) and provisions two disposable PostgreSQL
81	databases via the `migrate-control` / `migrate-project` one-shot services.
82	Subsequent runs can drop `--build` unless `package.json`/`pnpm-lock.yaml`
83	changed.
84	
85	## Shutdown and reset
86	
87	```bash
88	docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml stop                              # stop, keep containers and data
89	docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --remove-orphans             # remove containers/network, KEEP data
90	docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --volumes --remove-orphans   # reset: DELETE this project's data
91	```
92	
93	The last command destroys both local databases and every stored
94	object. Read ["Persistence, lifecycle, and reset"](#persistence-lifecycle-and-reset)
95	below for the full lifecycle table, exactly what a reset deletes, and
96	how to recreate the stack afterward.
97	
98	## Service graph and addresses
99	
100	| Service | Role | Published to host? | Internal address | Notes |
101	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
102	| `nginx` | Reverse proxy | **Yes** — `127.0.0.1:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT:-8080}` | `nginx:80` | The only entry point for `web`/`api`. |
103	| `web` | Next.js dev | No | `web:3000` | Reached only via `nginx`. |
104	| `api` | Hono dev | No | `api:3001` | Reached only via `nginx`'s `/api/` prefix — never published directly, per this task's "health/readiness only through the proxy" requirement. |
105	| `worker` | Worker dev (`tsx watch`) | n/a (no listener) | n/a | See "Known limitations." |
106	| `postgres` | Control DB + project-test DB | No | `postgres:5432` | Two databases, one server — see "Database isolation." |
107	| `migrate-control` / `migrate-project` | One-shot provisioning | n/a | n/a | Run once at startup, exit 0, do not stay running. |
108	| `storage` | SeaweedFS S3 gateway | **Yes** — `127.0.0.1:${SEAWEEDFS_S3_PORT:-8333}` | `storage:8333` | Development-only endpoint; no app adapter consumes it. |
109	| `mailhog` | Mail capture, web UI | **Yes** (UI only) — `127.0.0.1:${MAILHOG_UI_PORT:-8025}` | `mailhog:8025` (UI), `mailhog:1025` (SMTP) | SMTP stays internal — nothing submits mail through it yet. |
110	
111	### Internal vs. host-facing vs. browser-public addresses
112	
113	- **Internal (Compose-only hostnames)**: `postgres:5432`, `api:3001`,
114	  `web:3000`, `storage:8333`/`9333`/`8888`, `mailhog:1025`. These resolve
115	  only inside the Compose network and are never reachable from the host
116	  browser or shell.
117	- **Host-facing (loopback-published)**: `127.0.0.1:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT}`,
118	  `127.0.0.1:${MAILHOG_UI_PORT}`, `127.0.0.1:${SEAWEEDFS_S3_PORT}` — reachable
119	  from the host machine (curl, a browser, a local S3 client) but bound to
120	  loopback only, never `0.0.0.0`, per this task's "bind published
121	  development ports to loopback" requirement.
122	- **Browser-public**: `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`, set to
123	  `http://localhost:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT:-8080}/api` — **not** the internal
124	  `api:3001` hostname. `apps/web/src/app/page.tsx`'s existing client-side
125	  `fetch(`${apiUrl}/health`)` call is unmodified; it now resolves through
126	  nginx's `/api/` prefix (stripped by nginx, reaching `apps/api` as
127	  `GET /health`) instead of a hostname the browser could never resolve.
128	  Because the page itself is also served through the same nginx origin,
129	  this fetch is **same-origin** — no cross-origin request, so the
130	  existing `API_CORS_ORIGIN` setting (still configured, defensively, as
131	  `http://localhost:${NGINX_HTTP_PORT}`) is not actually exercised in
132	  normal use.
133	
134	## Clean-checkout startup
135	
136	Each of `docker/web/Dockerfile`, `docker/api/Dockerfile`, and
137	`docker/worker/Dockerfile`:
138	
139	1. Copies only manifests first, then runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`
140	   (cached across source-only changes).
141	2. Copies the rest of the workspace and runs `pnpm --filter @relis/config
142	   build` once, baking an initial `dist/`.
143	3. At container start, the `command:` override in `docker-compose.yml`
144	   runs `pnpm --filter @relis/config build` **again** before the real
145	   `dev` command — because, as established in
146	   [the inventory doc](local-stack-inventory.md#3-exact-existing-application-commands-and-source-references),
147	   individual `dev`/`start`/`migrate` commands do **not** rebuild
148	   `@relis/config` themselves, and its `package.json` `exports` resolve
149	   only to `./dist/*`. Rebuilding on every start keeps that dist current
150	   with whatever `packages/config/src` the development bind-mount (below)
151	   is currently showing, even though the image already baked one copy.
152	
153	## Development mounts
154	
155	Only **source** subdirectories are bind-mounted for live editing —
156	`apps/web/src`, `apps/web/public`, `apps/api/src`, `apps/worker/src`, and
157	`packages/config/src` (into whichever of the three app containers consume
158	it). `node_modules`, `dist`, and `.next` are **never** mounted: they stay
159	whatever the image build produced, so a bind mount can never hide an
160	installed dependency or a required build artifact. This also sidesteps a
161	harder problem a whole-repository bind mount would create: on a genuinely
162	clean host checkout, `node_modules` doesn't exist yet (it's gitignored),
163	so mounting the entire repository over the image's `/app` would hide the
164	image's own already-installed `node_modules` with nothing. Mounting only
165	`src/`/`public/` avoids that entirely.
166	
167	## Database isolation
168	
169	`migrate-control` and `migrate-project` each run the **existing**
170	`packages/database/src/migrate.ts` entry point, unchanged, against one
171	target each:
172	
173	- `migrate-control` → `CONTROL_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://.../relis_control`
174	- `migrate-project` → `PROJECT_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://.../relis_project_example`
175	
176	Both URLs are built from `POSTGRES_USER`/`POSTGRES_PASSWORD` plus their
177	own database name — never from each other, and never substituted for one
178	another. `docker/postgres/init/01-create-project-test-database.sh` creates
179	the second database (`relis_project_example` by default) alongside the
180	official postgres image's own creation of `POSTGRES_DB`
181	(`relis_control`). Neither Prisma schema defines a model, so this proves
182	the two-target connection contract, not a business schema — consistent
183	with this task's "without adding business models" boundary.
184	
185	## Persistence, lifecycle, and reset
186	
187	Implements local sub-issue [02.03 — Configure local persistent volumes
188	and exclude them from version
189	control](../../../context/notion-tasks/sub-issues/02-03.md). Everything
190	below describes **local, disposable development data only** — there is no
191	production target, no external volume, and no backup or restore
192	mechanism anywhere in this stack.
193	
194	### What persists, and where
195	
196	Two Docker **named volumes** hold every byte of persistent state. One
197	PostgreSQL server with one physical volume holds *both* logical
198	databases — deliberately: a container or volume per database is not a
199	requirement of this stack and is not implemented.
200	
201	| Owning service | Container path | Backed by | Holds | Disposable? |
202	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
203	| `postgres` | `/var/lib/postgresql/data` | named volume `<project>_postgres-data` | The whole PostgreSQL cluster: **both** logical databases (the Control DB `relis_control` *and* the project-test database `relis_project_example`), plus server-wide state (roles, WAL, the `postgres`/`template*` databases). | Yes |
204	| `storage` | `/data` | named volume `<project>_storage-data` | SeaweedFS's entire single-node state in one directory: master metadata, volume (object) files, and filer metadata — i.e. every bucket and non-production object. | Yes |
205	
206	`<project>` is the Compose project name (see "Project scoping" below).
207	With the default startup from this directory that is `relis`, so the two
208	real volume names are `relis_postgres-data` and `relis_storage-data`.
209	
210	Everything else mounted into a container is **configuration or source,
211	never generated data**:
212	
213	| Owning service | Container path | Backed by | Kind |
214	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
215	| `postgres` | `/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d` | `./docker/postgres/init` (read-only) | Committed first-init SQL. |
216	| `storage` | `/etc/seaweedfs/s3-identities.json` | `./docker/storage/s3-identities.json` (read-only) | Committed development-only S3 identity. |
217	| `nginx` | `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` | `./docker/nginx/nginx.conf` (read-only) | Committed proxy routing. |
218	| `api` | `/app/apps/api/src` | `./apps/api/src` | Committed source, mounted for live reload. |
219	| `web` | `/app/apps/web/src`, `/app/apps/web/public` | `./apps/web/src`, `./apps/web/public` | Committed source/assets, mounted for live reload. |
220	| `worker` | `/app/apps/worker/src` | `./apps/worker/src` | Committed source, mounted for live reload. |
221	| `api`, `web`, `worker` | `/app/packages/config/src` | `./packages/config/src` | Committed shared-config source (see "Development mounts"). |
222	
223	Generated **application** artifacts — `node_modules`, `dist`, `.next` —
224	are never mounted at all: each lives only inside its image/container
225	layer (see "Development mounts" above) and is rebuilt from the committed
226	lockfile and source. They are therefore not persistent across container
227	recreation either, and recreating a container re-derives them.
228	
229	The consequence worth stating explicitly: **no service bind-mounts a
230	writable data directory out of this repository.** Database and object
231	data cannot become a tracked repository artifact, because no path in the
232	working tree ever holds any. `tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence.test.ts`
233	asserts this directly against the resolved Compose configuration, which
234	is a stronger guarantee than an ignore rule.
235	
236	`.gitignore` covers the remaining cases: real environment files
237	(`.env`, `.env.*`, with `.env.example` the committed exception),
238	generated build output (`dist`, `.next`, `node_modules`), coverage, test
239	run output (`test-results/`, `playwright-report/`, `blob-report/`), and —
240	defensively — the generated-artifact directories the required structure
241	reserves at `storage/uploads/`, `storage/exports/`, and `storage/temp/`
242	(those do not exist yet and no application adapter writes to them).
243	`tests/integration/docker-compose/persistence-ignore-rules.test.ts`
244	verifies all of it with read-only Git commands, and additionally asserts
245	that no ignore pattern is broad enough to shadow a tracked source file.
246	
247	### Project scoping
248	
249	Compose prefixes each declared volume with the project name, so the
250	project name alone decides which data a startup reuses:
251	
252	| Startup | Project name | Volumes used |
253	| --- | --- | --- |
254	| `docker compose up` from this directory | `relis` (the directory name) | `relis_postgres-data`, `relis_storage-data` |
255	| `docker compose -p other up` | `other` | `other_postgres-data`, `other_storage-data` |
256	| An integration test's disposable project | `relis-persist-<random>` etc. | `relis-persist-<random>_postgres-data`, … |
257	
258	Consequences, all verified rather than assumed:
259	
260	- **A normal startup reuses the intended development volumes.** Running
261	  `docker compose up` again — with or without `--build`, and after any
262	  number of `docker compose down` cycles — reattaches `relis_*` and
263	  finds the previous data.
264	- **Separate Compose projects cannot share a data volume.** Neither
265	  volume is `external: true`, neither declares an explicit `name:`, and
266	  nothing points at a path outside the repository or at a
267	  machine-specific location, so two projects can only ever resolve to
268	  different volume names. `persistence.test.ts` proves this with a
269	  second, independently-named Compose project whose own fixture row is
270	  invisible from the first and survives the first's reset.
271	- The Compose **network** is likewise per-project: it is declared as
272	  `${COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME:-relis}-net`, and Compose V2 feeds `-p` into
273	  that interpolation (confirmed: `docker compose -p X config` resolves
274	  the network name to `X-net`), so a `-p`-scoped run does not reuse the
275	  default stack's network either.
276	- No production endpoint, external volume, or absolute host path appears
277	  anywhere in `docker-compose.yml`; every bind source is a
278	  repository-relative path.
279	
280	### Lifecycle operations
281	
282	Always pass the project and file explicitly — `-p <project> -f
283	docker-compose.yml` — so a command can never act on a different project
284	than intended. (`docker compose` infers the project from the current
285	directory's name when `-p` is omitted; being explicit costs nothing and
286	removes the ambiguity entirely, which matters most for the last row.)
287	
288	| Goal | Command | Containers | Named volumes | Data |
289	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
290	| **Stop**, keeping containers and data | `docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml stop` | Stopped, **kept** | Kept | **Kept** |
291	| **Start** again (same containers) | `docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml start` | Restarted in place | Kept | **Kept** |
292	| **Restart** in one step | `docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml restart` | Restarted in place | Kept | **Kept** |
293	| **Remove containers and the network**, keeping data | `docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --remove-orphans` | **Removed** | **Kept** | **Kept** |
294	| Recreate after that removal | `docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml up -d` | Newly created | Reattached | **Kept** |
295	| **Reset** — delete this project's disposable data | `docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --volumes --remove-orphans` | **Removed** | **DELETED** | **DESTROYED** |
296	
297	The only difference between the fourth row and the last is the
298	`--volumes` flag. That flag is the entire reset.
299	
300	### ⚠️ Reset destroys data — read before running it
301	
302	`docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml down --volumes --remove-orphans`
303	**permanently and irreversibly deletes**:
304	
305	- `relis_postgres-data` — and with it **both** logical databases at
306	  once: the Control DB (`relis_control`) *and* the project-test database
307	  (`relis_project_example`), plus every table, row, and role on that
308	  server. They share one volume; there is no way to reset one and keep
309	  the other.
310	- `relis_storage-data` — and with it **every bucket and object** in the
311	  local SeaweedFS instance.
312	
313	It does **not** touch: your source code, `.env`, any other Compose
314	project's containers or volumes, or the built images (those are a build
315	cache, removed separately and deliberately if ever wanted). There is no
316	backup, no snapshot, and no undo — this stack intentionally implements
317	none, because its data is local and disposable by design.
318	
319	Substitute the real project name for `relis` if you started the stack
320	with a different `-p`. If you are unsure what a reset would delete, list
321	it first — a read-only check:
322	
323	```bash
324	docker volume ls --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=relis
325	```
326	
327	Never reset as part of ordinary startup: `up`, `up --build`, `stop`,
328	`start`, `restart`, and `down` (without `--volumes`) all keep data, and
329	that is the normal path.
330	
331	**Do not** use broad commands to clean up instead. `docker system prune`,
332	`docker volume prune`, `docker builder prune --all`, a bare
333	`docker volume rm` against a guessed name, or deleting a directory with
334	`rm -rf` all reach beyond this project and can destroy unrelated
335	containers, volumes, and other developers' or other projects' data. The
336	scoped `down --volumes` above is the only reset this stack needs, which
337	is why **no reset script is provided**: the existing Compose commands and
338	this table are sufficient, and a script would add a second, more
339	dangerous way to do the same thing.
340	
341	### Clean recreation after a reset
342	
343	Everything needed to come back is committed; no manual data restoration
344	step exists or is required.
345	
346	```bash
347	docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml up -d --build
348	```
349	
350	That alone recreates, from committed configuration plus the documented
351	local setup (`cp .env.example .env`, see "Prerequisites"):
352	
353	1. Both named volumes, empty, under the same names.
354	2. An initialised PostgreSQL cluster. Because the data directory is empty
355	   again, the official image runs its own first-init sequence: it creates
356	   `POSTGRES_DB` (the Control DB) and then runs everything in
357	   `/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d`, so
358	   `docker/postgres/init/01-create-project-test-database.sh` recreates
359	   the project-test database too.
360	3. A fresh single-node SeaweedFS instance with no buckets and no objects.
361	4. `migrate-control` and `migrate-project`, each running the existing
362	   migration entry point against its own target (see "Database
363	   isolation").
364	
365	Verify with the same read-only commands used to inspect any startup —
366	`docker compose -p relis -f docker-compose.yml ps` and the `/api/health`
367	endpoint through nginx.
368	
369	**Honest limitations of "recreated":**
370	
371	- **The databases come back empty, and that is all they can be.** Both
372	  `packages/database/prisma/control/schema.prisma` and
373	  `.../project/schema.prisma` define **zero models** and have **no
374	  `migrations/` directory**, so `migrate-control`/`migrate-project` have
375	  nothing to apply: they validate the connection contract and exit 0.
376	  Recreation restores *databases*, not a schema — there is no business
377	  schema to restore, and none is added here.
378	- **No seed data of any kind.** Nothing repopulates application content
379	  after a reset; any fixture you had is gone for good. Test fixtures are
380	  created by the tests that need them.
381	- **No backup or restore.** Not implemented, not planned in this slice.
382	  If local data matters to you, do not reset.
383	- **`docker/postgres/init/` only runs on a genuinely first init** — i.e.
384	  against an empty data directory. Changing `POSTGRES_DB` or
385	  `PROJECT_TEST_DB_NAME` while `relis_postgres-data` still exists does
386	  **not** create the newly-named database; the init scripts are simply
387	  not re-run. Either create it manually or reset the volume (destroying
388	  the existing data) for the new name to take effect.
389	- **No per-project provisioning.** `relis_project_example` is a single
390	  disposable project-test target, not a per-project database factory.
391	  Creating a database per real review project is a separate, unimplemented
392	  feature.
393	- **A volume's on-disk format belongs to the image that wrote it.** Data
394	  written by `postgres:17-alpine` or `chrislusf/seaweedfs:3.71` is not
395	  guaranteed readable after a major version change of either image; a
396	  reset is the expected remedy in that case, since this data is
397	  disposable.

399	## Known limitations (read before relying on this stack)
400	
401	- **`apps/worker` does not process jobs, in any mode.** Its `dev` command
402	  (`tsx watch`) keeps the container's process alive (the watch supervisor
403	  stays running after the wrapped script's own log-and-return), but that
404	  liveness is **not** evidence of job processing — there is no queue
405	  consumer. The background-job backend (`pg-boss` vs. `BullMQ`) remains
406	  undecided (`context/stack.yml`); no Redis or other BullMQ-only
407	  dependency was added here on an assumption. `worker` intentionally has
408	  **no Compose healthcheck** — fabricating one would misrepresent this.
409	- **No application storage or mail adapter exists.** `storage` (SeaweedFS)
410	  and `mailhog` are real, running infrastructure services — reachable,
411	  credentialed (storage), and usable for manual inspection — but nothing
412	  in `apps/api`/`apps/worker` talks to either yet. Implementing those
413	  adapters is explicitly out of scope for this sub-issue.
414	- **Image tags: verified by real execution.** `postgres:17-alpine`,
415	  `nginx:1.27-alpine`, `mailhog/mailhog:v1.0.1`, and
416	  `chrislusf/seaweedfs:3.71` all pulled successfully from Docker Hub
417	  during the sub-issue #47 real verification. No longer a documentation
418	  caveat.
419	- **`mailhog` intentionally has no Compose `healthcheck:`.** MailHog's
420	  official image is commonly built as a minimal/near-scratch Go binary
421	  with no shell or `wget` bundled. Rather than ship a healthcheck command
422	  that might simply fail with "not found" (and be misread as "the
423	  service is unhealthy"), readiness is instead polled with a plain HTTP
424	  request from the test client's own side (`waitForHttpOk` in
425	  `packages/test-utils/src/docker-compose.ts`, used by
426	  `stack-smoke.test.ts`) — confirmed working this way against the real
427	  container.
428	- **Two healthcheck defects were found and fixed by real verification**
429	  (both reproducible, not transient):
430	  - `nginx`'s healthcheck used `http://localhost/nginx-health`.
431	    `nginx:alpine`'s musl resolver returns `::1` before `127.0.0.1` for
432	    "localhost" inside the container, and this `nginx.conf`'s `listen
433	    80;` only binds IPv4 — so the healthcheck connection was refused even
434	    though nginx was serving correctly. Fixed by targeting `127.0.0.1`
435	    explicitly. Confirmed to not affect host access or
436	    container-to-container traffic (neither ever addresses this service
437	    as "localhost").
438	  - `storage` (SeaweedFS)'s healthcheck targeted the master's
439	    `/cluster/status` on port 9333, which becomes ready slightly before
440	    its S3 gateway (port 8333) finishes connecting to the filer
441	    internally — confirmed via that container's own startup logs. Docker
442	    reported "healthy" in that narrow window, and a real signed PUT
443	    issued right after got the connection closed by the server with no
444	    HTTP response at all (`SocketError: other side closed`). Fixed by
445	    checking the S3 gateway's own port directly (`nc -z 127.0.0.1 8333`
446	    — BusyBox `wget`'s exit code cannot distinguish "got a 403" from
447	    "connection refused," and `curl` is not present in this image, both
448	    confirmed by direct inspection).
449	- **The SeaweedFS SigV4 signer: verified against a live server.**
450	  `packages/test-utils/src/s3-sigv4.ts` implements AWS Signature Version
451	  4 (Node's built-in `crypto` only, no new dependency). A real signed PUT
452	  + GET round-trip against the actual running `storage` container
453	  succeeded byte-for-byte (after the healthcheck fix above, and after
454	  adding an explicit `createBucket` call before the upload — see
455	  `packages/test-utils/src/s3-sigv4.ts` and `stack-smoke.test.ts`;
456	  SeaweedFS auto-vivifies a bucket on first PUT, but explicit creation
457	  does not rely on that server-specific behavior).
458	  `docker/storage/s3-identities.json`'s schema
459	  (`identities`/`credentials`/`actions`) and the `-s3.config` flag both
460	  worked as written — no changes were needed there.
461	- **A dependency-unavailable Prisma failure reveals the target host,
462	  port, database name, and schema — but not the embedded credentials.**
463	  Reproduced directly: stopping `postgres` and running `migrate-control`
464	  against it produces Prisma's own real error —
465	  `` Datasource "db": PostgreSQL database "relis_control", schema "public" at "postgres:5432"
466	  Error: P1001: Can't reach database server at `postgres:5432` `` — which
467	  is **not** as strictly secret-free as this project's own
468	  `ConfigValidationError` diagnostics (which never reveal any part of a
469	  value, only variable names/categories): it does echo the database name
470	  and host:port parsed out of the connection string. It does **not**
471	  echo the username or password. This is real Prisma CLI behavior,
472	  unchanged and out of scope to alter here; documented precisely rather
473	  than assumed.
474	- **Graceful shutdown: observed clean across every real test run, exact
475	  signal chain not individually instrumented.** `docker compose down`
476	  completed successfully (containers stopped and removed, no forced
477	  escalation observed) across roughly a dozen real `composeUp`/
478	  `cleanupComposeProject` cycles during verification, including after
479	  deliberately-failing scenarios. Whether `pnpm`'s own process forwards
480	  `SIGTERM` to the underlying `tsx watch`/`next dev`/`run.mjs` child via
481	  the same path as `apps/web/scripts/run.mjs`'s own signal-forwarding
482	  logic specifically (as opposed to Docker's own escalation to `SIGKILL`
483	  after its stop grace period) was not individually isolated or timed.
